statements.quote: We have our first live event on the Sunday night before JPM Healthcare 2024. It’s called Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment 2024, and you should get your ticket now!
statements.context: Opening paragraph of the gabapentin essay (2023-11-08). The author announces the newsletter's first live event, Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment 2024 (RAMHT), to be held the Sunday night before JPM Healthcare 2024 in San Francisco.
statements.horizon_text: the Sunday night before JPM Healthcare 2024
statements.note: Own-event announcement; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL (RAMHT). Repeated in later posts of this packet.

statements.quote: When fines are less than the profits, expect the behavior to continue.
statements.context: Closing argument of the gabapentin essay. After recounting Warner-Lambert/Pfizer's off-label marketing of Neurontin for bipolar disorder and about $945 million in settlements against $1b-$2.7b annual sales, the author expects predatory off-label marketing by drug makers to continue as long as fines stay below profits.
statements.note: General conditional expectation about industry behavior; no named future case. Only loosely verifiable.

statements.quote: There are more of these. I’ll release them in this feed.
statements.context: Intro to episode 1 of the author's archival 2020 pandemic podcast 'Remotely Possible', republished in the newsletter feed. The author says more episodes exist and commits to releasing them in this feed.
statements.note: Content-release plan for own newsletter; trivial. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: this lack of focus on mistrust engendered as a public health risk is an enduring legacy
statements.context: The author criticizes how the pandemic was explained to the public and claims the failure to treat engendered mistrust as a public health risk is an enduring legacy, i.e. that mistrust will persist as a public health problem.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense assessment with implied persistence. Not a dated or measurable call.

statements.quote: a jury awarded a ton of money to the family, leaving years of appeals, recriminations, and a family bereft in its wake
statements.context: Opening of an essay on factitious disorder by proxy prompted by the Netflix documentary 'Take Care of Maya'. On 2023-11-09 a Florida jury awarded Maya Kowalski's family $211 million against Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital; the author states the verdict leaves years of appeals ahead.
statements.note: Implicit legal forecast: appeals will run for years. The author explicitly declines to weigh in on the legal merits.

statements.quote: We are predictable. We will avoid “not knowing”— if we don’t build trust first .
statements.context: Author's retrospective on pandemic communication: humans predictably avoid uncertainty and take the path of most certainty even if it is bad, unless trust is built first. Framed as a general, conditional prediction about public behavior.
statements.note: Near-truism about human behavior; conditional. Same idea as 'They're going to take the path of most certainty.' Logged for recall.

statements.quote: A cure for depression – in the strong sense of the word cure – may just be too good to be true.
statements.context: Question 10 of the author's Q&A with Awais Aftab, M.D. (Psychiatry at the Margins): 'Would anyone believe a cure for depression existed even if it did?' Aftab answers that a true cure for depression may be too good to be true, comparing it to curing pain.
statements.note: Third-party (interviewee) forecast; the author neither endorses nor disputes it.

statements.quote: We can certainly treat depression, and we can get to a point where we can treat it very well, but I think there will always be this need to engage and grapple with depression as a human phenomenon.
statements.context: Same answer by Aftab (Q10). He expects treatment of depression to become very good but the need to engage with depression as a human phenomenon to persist indefinitely.
statements.note: Third-party (interviewee) compound claim: treatment will improve; the phenomenon will not disappear.

statements.quote: But depression itself, as a broad clinical phenomenon existing on a continuum with ordinary misery, may be here to stay.
statements.context: Same answer by Aftab (Q10), closing line. He distinguishes extreme pathological depression (treatable and preventable) from broad depression on a continuum with ordinary misery, which he expects to persist.
statements.note: Third-party (interviewee); restates the 'always be this need' claim.

statements.quote: Extreme states of depression are so disabling and impairing that they are recognizably pathological, and there is no reason why we cannot find highly effective interventions to treat and prevent them.
statements.context: Same answer by Aftab (Q10). He expects highly effective interventions for extreme, pathological depression to be findable, in contrast to a cure for depression in general.
statements.note: Third-party (interviewee) hedged optimism about future treatments; undated.

statements.quote: We will have an in-person, live, pre-JPM Healthcare event in San Fransisco on January 7th, 2024!
statements.context: Closing plug of the Observational AI post. Announces the RAMHT 2024 live event on January 7, 2024 in San Francisco before JPM Healthcare, with website and Eventbrite links.
statements.note: Repeat of the RAMHT 2024 event announcement; own-event, coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I don’t use AI to write because, frankly , it is not a good writer (yet).
statements.context: In the Observational AI post the author explains he writes without generative AI because it is not yet a good writer; the '(yet)' implies he expects generative AI to become a good writer.
statements.note: Implied forecast carried only by '(yet)'; borderline.

statements.quote: Since it’s so good at cranking out endless content, it risks a data pollution effect.
statements.context: Section 'Observational AI isn't a Polluter'. The author argues generative AI output fed back into training degrades model performance, so generative AI risks polluting language data; Observational AI does not carry this risk.
statements.note: Hedged risk statement about future model degradation from synthetic data.

statements.quote: And I think the ability to observe, measure, and understand at scale is where my dime, at least in biomedical science, comes down for the immediate future.
statements.context: Thesis of the post 'Is Observational AI the Next Big Thing?'. The author bets that AI for observation and measurement (his 'Observational AI': passive monitoring in Spravato sessions, SAINT targeting, TDetect tardive dyskinesia rating, Nightware, PRISM) rather than generative AI is where biomedical science goes in the immediate future.
statements.note: Author admits bias (he works on these studies). Direction-of-field call; loosely verifiable. Fermata, Acacia, Videra are own organizations.

statements.quote: But human minds are bad at math, and math-ready AI? That has the potential to solve its miscalculation problem.
statements.context: Discussing reports that OpenAI's Q* model made progress on math. The author says AI is currently bad at math but math-capable AI could solve its own miscalculation problem, unlike humans.
statements.note: Hedged capability forecast.

statements.quote: The threat to human life might be artificial intelligence in the future . It might be dangerous.
statements.context: Core argument of the essay: AI might become a threat to human life in the future, but the actual everyday threat is human intelligence.
statements.note: Hedged concession; the author's main point is that human intelligence is the present danger.

statements.quote: Human terror is a feature that allows us to survive and will be baked into the linguistic DNA of artificial intelligence.
statements.context: Arguing that AI is built on human language and therefore inherits human traits, the author predicts human terror and fear responses will be baked into artificial intelligence.
statements.note: Undated trait forecast about AI systems.

statements.quote: Computers don't get terrified right now, as far as I know. They're going to learn from us.
statements.context: Same passage. The author predicts AI systems will learn human traits, including fear-driven behavior, from human data, citing the Sam Altman firing as an example of what they are learning now.
statements.note: Companion to the 'baked into the linguistic DNA' claim.

statements.quote: We're going to need some treaty or plan to deal with it.
statements.context: After 'Human intelligence is tremendously dangerous', the author says humanity will need a treaty or plan to deal with dangerous human intelligence, 'until something better comes along'.
statements.note: Rhetorical, tongue-in-cheek inversion of AI-treaty talk; 'it' is human intelligence. Borderline predictive reading.

statements.quote: Now that we've created artificial intelligence, it is a matter of time before artificial general intelligence is on the team. It's going to happen. I don't think we can stop it.
statements.context: Near the end of the essay prompted by the OpenAI board firing Sam Altman over reported AGI fears (Q*). The author asserts AGI is inevitable and cannot be stopped.
statements.note: Compound: AGI will arrive; it cannot be stopped. No date given.

statements.quote: I can guarantee you—humans will act crazy . I can't guarantee the same about artificial general intelligence.
statements.context: Closing section. The author contrasts the certainty of future human irrationality with uncertainty about how artificial general intelligence will behave.
statements.note: Near-truism about human behavior; logged for recall.

statements.quote: I bet all the people who are bad at math could still figure out that firing Sam Altman when he created a $90 billion valuation company with an additional $10 billion from Microsoft would not fly with either Microsoft or anybody else who cared about the money
statements.context: The author argues the OpenAI board failed to 'do the math': firing Sam Altman would not be accepted by Microsoft or other money-interested parties. Written 2023-11-23, after the firing; the post already calls the firing a failed landing.
statements.note: Retrospective judgment about a decision already made; logged for completeness with forward_looking false.
